obs_text: The characteristic is named from Greek argos/argia, 'idle/idleness' — the state of being unproductive, without work or occupation. The name signals essential inertness: a failure to be operative or engaged, rather than active wrongdoing per se.

Greek argos (a-ergos, 'not-working') at the definitional level denotes 'not working the ground,' hence idle, lazy, unemployed, or (of things) unwrought/unproductive - money lying idle, land lying fallow. Applied to persons it moves from literal non-labor to moral censure of laziness.

The term carries a privative/negative-relational implication built into its etymology (alpha-privative + ergon 'work'): it defines a person or thing by absence of due activity, implying a constitutional failure to fulfill an expected functional role.

Primary Greek term argos (a-privative + ergon, 'work') shows the root meaning 'without work.' No distinct Hebrew equivalent is in view here (this is an NT-only cluster term); the Greek root meaning centers on absence of productive activity.

The vocabulary arc runs from concrete economic idleness (unemployed persons, fallow fields, unworked money) through social censure (busybody idlers going house to house, 1Tim 5:13; lazy gluttons, Titus 1:12) to abstract theological application (useless/ineffective faith without works, Jas 2:20) — showing a single root sense of 'non-functioning' extended across physical, social, and spiritual domains.
This occurrence matches the term's usual NT sense of habitual laziness/idleness (as in Mt.20.3,6; Tit.1.12), here specifically producing gossip and meddling; no divergence from its ordinary use.

Grammatical range is adjectival (A-NPF etc.), used substantivally ('idlers') or predicatively ('is no trouble', 'is useless'). This shows the characteristic operates as a descriptor of persons, things, or states rather than as a verbal action in its own right.
The vocabulary here does not itself distinguish disposition versus act; argos describes a state/condition (being unproductive) rather than differentiating received versus given aspects.

The structural opposite is implicit in the root itself: ergos/energos ('working, active, effective'), against which argos is formed by negation (a-privative). No separate lexeme is supplied among these sources beyond this internal contrast.

The person-type term is embedded in the adjective itself used substantivally: 'the idle one/idlers' (hai argoi), as in 1Tim 5:13 and Titus 1:12's 'lazy gluttons' - the word doubles as noun and adjective without a distinct separate person-noun.
None - no supplication/seeking term is associated with idleness/uselessness; this characteristic is not something sought from another but a condition observed or censured.

This is a purely Greek/NT term with no Hebrew counterpart surfaced in these sources; continuity is thus intra-Greek (classical Greek usage of argos for fallow land/idle money carries directly into NT moral usage for idle persons and useless faith), showing semantic development from economic/agricultural sense to ethical-spiritual censure.
None - argos is a long-attested classical Greek term (Homer onward), not a NT-period coinage.
ἀγανάκτησις names 'indignation', a term signalling roused displeasure/vexation at wrongdoing rather than simple sadness.

LSJ's earliest sense is literal physical irritation (e.g. teething pain) before the metaphorical extension to 'vexation'; both Thucydides and this verse use the developed sense of moral vexation/indignation.
The term's implication is relational -- indignation directed at the wrongdoing itself, evidence of the Corinthians' changed moral orientation following godly grief.
Root ἀγανακτέω/ἀγανάκτησις shows physical irritation extending to vexation; attested from Plato (Phaedrus) through Thucydides prior to NT use, so this is not an NT coinage.
Occurs as a noun (N-ASF), this being its sole NT occurrence, naming the state of indignation as one item in a list of inner responses.
Semantic range moves from literal bodily irritation (LSJ's teething example) to moral/emotional vexation and, of God, wrath -- here used of the Corinthians' own righteous displeasure at the offense.
ἁγνός names 'pure/chaste/innocent', a term rooted in cultic holiness language (related to ἅγιος), signalling ritual and moral purity together.

LSJ traces ἁγνός from Homer through classical usage: originally of things/places 'hallowed', then of persons 'chaste, undefiled', and 'pure from blood/guiltless'; Mounce/meaning tree confirm 'pure, chaste, innocent' -- both moral and ritual senses attested.
The term implies a constitutional (status-declaring) sense here -- the Corinthians are declared/proved clear of guilt in the matter, the culminating verdict of the whole list of responses.
ἁγνός root relates to ἅγιος, attested from Homer onward meaning 'pure, chaste, holy', long predating NT usage.
Occurs as an adjective (A-APM) describing the Corinthians' proven status, consistent with the term's regular adjectival use to qualify persons as pure/guiltless.
Semantic range spans cultic 'hallowed', divine 'chaste/holy', and human 'guiltless from blood/undefiled' (LSJ); here the sense is forensic-moral, 'proved innocent/guiltless in the matter'.
ἐκδίκησις names 'vengeance/punishment', built on ἐκ + δίκη, signalling justice carried out to completion against a wrong.

LSJ shows ἐκδίκησις meaning 'avenging' with the idiom ἐκδίκησιν ποιεῖσθαι, 'to give satisfaction'; Mounce/meaning tree confirm 'vengeance, punishment, retributive justice' -- both stress the act of setting a wrong right through retribution.
The term implies a directional, corrective relation -- readiness to see wrong punished/set right, here evidenced by the Corinthians willingly submitting to discipline as proof of sincerity.
ἐκδίκησις root is ἐκ + δίκη ('justice, right'), attested in Polybius before NT use, meaning full/completed retribution or legal satisfaction.
Occurs as a noun (N-ASF) naming the readiness for retributive action as the climax of the list of responses to godly grief.

Semantic range covers legal remedy, satisfaction, and vengeance/punishment (LSJ); here used of the Corinthians' willingness to see the offender justly dealt with, part of a suite of proofs of repentance.
ἐπιπόθησις names 'longing after', built on ἐπί + ποθέω, signalling a strong directed yearning rather than a passive wish.

LSJ attests ἐπιπόθησις only in NT and near-contemporary usage (2Cor.7.7, Aquila's Ezek.23.11) meaning 'longing after' with genitive object; the meaning tree confirms 'earnest desire, strong affection'.

The term carries a relational implication of desire directed toward restoring a relationship -- here the Corinthians' longing is directed toward Paul/reconciliation, part of the fruits of godly grief.

ἐπιπόθησις root meaning is 'longing after' (ἐπί + ποθέω); LSJ's only citations are NT and a near-contemporary translation of Ezekiel, showing the noun form itself is very rare pre-NT though the verb ποθέω is classical.

Occurs as an abstract noun (N-ASF) naming the state/emotion of longing, one of only two NT occurrences (both 2 Cor.7), showing the term operates as a named inner disposition rather than a verb of acting.

Semantic range is narrow and intensive: 'earnest desire, strong affection' directed toward a person or restored relationship, here listed among a cluster of intense emotional responses produced by godly grief.
ζῆλος names 'zeal', a term that can signal either ardent devoted concern or, negatively, jealousy/rivalry -- its name signals an intense emotional energy that can move in either moral direction.

LSJ shows ζῆλος ranging from jealousy/rivalry (Hesiod, Sophocles) to eager emulation and fervour/zeal (LXX, NT); Mounce lists both the positive 'ardent concern' and negative 'jealousy, envy, rage' senses -- the term is definitionally dual-valenced.

In this list of Corinthian responses the term implies zeal directed toward setting a wrong right -- a constitutional (character-revealing) implication, evidencing genuine repentance rather than mere regret.
Greek ζῆλος root sense is heated/boiling passion (compare ζέω), yielding both 'jealousy' and 'zeal/emulation' depending on direction of the passion's object.
Occurs as a noun (N-ASM) naming the emotion/quality itself, consistent with its use across the NT as an abstract noun for zeal or jealousy rather than a verb form.

LSJ documents an unusually wide range: jealousy/envy, eager rivalry/emulation, ambition, pride/honour, fervour, and even personified deity -- here used in the positive 'zeal for right conduct' sense as one of the godly-grief-produced responses.

The negative pole of this term's own semantic range (jealousy/envy, φθόνος-adjacent) functions as its own structural opposite depending on direction -- LSJ explicitly couples ζῆλος with φθόνος as near-synonym in the negative sense, showing the term itself contains its own antithetical pole.
λυπέω names 'to grieve/cause sorrow', signalling an act that produces distress in the one affected, whether physical or emotional.

LSJ shows λυπέω used from Homer onward for causing pain of body or mind, and in historians for military 'harassing'; the passive means 'be grieved/distressed' -- here the passive-sense noun phrase 'godly grief' functions as the cause of the list of responses.
Qualified here by 'godly' (κατὰ θεόν), the term's directional implication is that this grief is oriented toward God -- a grief that produces repentance rather than mere distress.
λυπέω is well-attested from Homer/Hesiod onward with senses ranging from physical distress to military harassment, long predating NT usage; the NT sense narrows to emotional/spiritual grief.
Occurs here as an infinitive/verbal noun form (V-APN, 'to grieve'), showing the term functioning as the verbal root-cause governing the whole list of resulting nouns (earnestness, eagerness, etc.).

Semantic range spans literal bodily pain (weight of armor) through emotional grief to military 'harassment'; here it is the qualified 'godly grief' that causally produces earnestness and the rest, showing an idiomatic causal use.

The characteristic is named from σπουδή (earnestness/diligence/zeal), the positive pole of the M67 cluster. The name signals energetic, focused application -- effort applied with urgency, whether physical haste or moral/spiritual earnestness.

The term carries a directional implication of movement toward a goal with urgency -- it names both the manner (swiftly) and the intensity (wholeheartedly) of an action or disposition, and functions relationally as evidence offered to others (2 Cor 7:11-12, 8:7-8) of inward sincerity.
Primary Greek term σπουδή, from σπεύδω 'to hasten'. Root meaning: hurried, urgent exertion, extending to earnest zeal and diligence. No Hebrew equivalent supplied in this cluster's data.

The full arc moves from concrete physical haste/speed, through general zealous exertion and attentiveness (including political/partisan zeal in classical usage), to an ethical-relational sense in the NT epistles where earnestness becomes visible proof of sincere character (repentance, love, generosity) offered for others to observe and judge.

In Mark.6.25 σπουδή retains its base literal sense of physical haste ('with haste' to the king) with no metaphorical shift. In 2Cor.7.11, 7.12, 8.7, 8.8 and Rom.12.11 the term shifts from physical speed to an ethical-relational nuance of demonstrable zeal/earnestness functioning as evidence of sincerity -- a marked shift from the base 'haste' gloss toward a virtue-term describing wholehearted moral engagement, distinctive to the Pauline corpus's use compared to the narrative/literal use in Mark.
This occurrence matches the term's usual NT sense of earnest diligence/zeal (cf. Rom.12.8,11; 2Cor.8.7,16) -- no divergence in nuance from its other occurrences.

σπουδή occurs here only as a noun (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-ASF, N-DSF across occurrences), naming a quality or state rather than the act itself; the related adverb σπουδαίως (G4709) supplies the manner-of-action form, showing the characteristic operates both as a describable quality possessed and as a manner in which action is carried out.

Semantic range spans literal physical haste/speed (Mark 6:25, 'with haste' to the king), zeal as attentive/earnest effort in relationships and undertakings (Rom 12:11, 'not lagging in zeal'), and a demonstrable, quasi-evidentiary sense -- earnestness that others can observe and that functions as proof of genuine character (2 Cor 7:11-12, 8:7-8, where σπουδή is offered as evidence of repentance and love alongside other virtues).
None distinct within this occurrence set; no separate agent-noun ('the zealous one') is attested among the given strongs for this cluster.

No Hebrew counterpart is supplied for this cluster's data; the term's development is intra-Greek, moving from classical usage denoting physical haste and zealous effort/political partisanship (LSJ) to a specifically Christian ethical usage in the NT epistles as a virtue demonstrating sincerity of repentance and love.
None. σπουδή is a well-established classical term (attested from Herodotus onward per LSJ), not coined in the NT period.
φόβος names 'fear', from φέβομαι (to flee in panic) -- its root signals fear as flight-response, later broadened to reverence/respect.

LSJ traces φόβος from Homeric 'panic flight' to generalized 'fear, terror' and further to 'awe, reverence' for a ruler or deity; Mounce confirms both 'fear, terror' and 'respect, reverence' senses -- the term spans a wide definitional arc.

Here the fear is relationally directed -- toward the consequences of wrongdoing and toward restoring right relationship with Paul/God, showing fear functioning as a moral corrective rather than mere terror.
φόβος root is φέβομαι, 'panic flight' in Homer, broadening to general 'fear/terror' and 'reverence' in classical and LXX usage well before the NT.
Occurs as a noun (N-ASM), one of many NT occurrences, here naming an inner state alongside indignation and longing as a fruit of godly grief.

Semantic range spans panic flight, terror, doubt/scruple, and reverential awe (LSJ); here the sense leans toward trembling concern for consequences, consistent with Mounce's 'trembling concern' gloss for 2Cor.7.15.
ἀδικέω names the act of doing wrong/injuring another; its root signals injustice as an act against another party rather than an inner disposition.
ἀδικέω names the act of doing wrong/injuring another; its root signals injustice as an act against another party rather than an inner disposition.
Greek ἀδικέω at the definitional level denotes being ἄδικος in action -- to wrong, injure, treat unjustly, whether legally, physically, or relationally.
Greek ἀδικέω at the definitional level denotes being ἄδικος in action -- to wrong, injure, treat unjustly, whether legally, physically, or relationally.
The name carries a relational, two-party implication: one who wrongs and one who is wronged, an act done TO another, not a solitary state.
The name carries a relational, two-party implication: one who wrongs and one who is wronged, an act done TO another, not a solitary state.
Greek ἀδικέω, from ἄδικος (not-just), root shows injustice as departure from δίκη (right, justice).
Greek ἀδικέω, from ἄδικος (not-just), root shows injustice as departure from δίκη (right, justice).

Arc runs from generic 'do wrong/be unjust' (active) through legal, medical (harm), and financial-defrauding senses, to passive 'be wronged' -- here narrowed to the specific interpersonal offense at Corinth.

Arc runs from generic 'do wrong/be unjust' (active) through legal, medical (harm), and financial-defrauding senses, to passive 'be wronged' -- here narrowed to the specific interpersonal offense at Corinth.
This occurrence matches the term's ordinary interpersonal sense (one party wrongs, another suffers wrong); no divergence from usual usage.

ἀδικέω occurs here as a substantival participle (the one who did wrong / the one who suffered wrong), showing the term operates verbally, cast into a person-designation via participial form.

Semantic range spans legal wrongdoing, physical injury/harm, and fraud/defrauding; here it operates in the interpersonal/legal sense of an offense done between two Corinthian parties.

No structural-opposite term for ἀδικέω is present in this verse's role list.
The verse itself supplies the person-type via participial substantive: 'the one who did the wrong' (ὁ ἀδικήσας).
No supplication/seeking term for this characteristic appears in this verse.
ἀδικέω is a standard classical Greek legal/ethical term (Herodotus, Plato, Demosthenes) continued unchanged into NT usage denoting wrongdoing between persons.
Not a NT coinage; well attested from 7th c. BC (Archilochus, Sappho) onward.

Earnestness here for the Corinthians' care for Paul matches σπουδή's usual sense of zealous devotion/earnest care seen elsewhere (e.g. Rom.12.11, 2Cor.7.11), no divergence.

σπουδή occurs here only as a noun (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-ASF, N-DSF across occurrences), naming a quality or state rather than the act itself; the related adverb σπουδαίως (G4709) supplies the manner-of-action form, showing the characteristic operates both as a describable quality possessed and as a manner in which action is carried out.

In the M67 programme this NT term names 'earnestness/diligence' (spoudē) -- signalling zealous, energetic application, whether to a task (2Pet 1:5, supplementing faith) or to caring for a person (2Cor 8:16, Titus's care for the Corinthians).

The vocabulary arc for G4710 spans literal haste, zealous exertion for a cause, esteem/good-will for a person, and religious zeal -- showing a full semantic range from physical urgency to relational devotion and moral effort, richer than the OT Aramaic administrative-thoroughness sense.

Occurrence in 2Cor.8.16 rendered 'earnest care' shifts the base gloss from generic diligence/effort toward relational solicitude -- here the nuance is God-given personal concern for the Corinthians placed in Titus's heart, a warmer relational register than the task-oriented 'make every effort' sense of 2Pet 1:5; impact is to frame diligence as compassionate advocacy rather than self-directed striving.

Semantic range includes literal haste/speed, zealous effort toward a task ('make every effort' 2Pet 1:5), esteem/goodwill toward a person, and religious zeal (Rom 12:11) -- an idiomatic extension from physical urgency to moral and relational earnestness.
γνῶσις names 'knowledge,' rooted in γινώσκω (to know) -- signaling an essential nature of cognitive apprehension, here of Christian truth.
Greek γνῶσις at the definitional level denotes knowing/knowledge, including higher or esoteric knowledge in later usage, and specifically Christian enlightenment in the NT.
The name carries a constitutional implication: knowledge as an inward cognitive possession that can be excelled in and increased, listed among a set of graces.
γνῶσις, from γινώσκω, root shows the act/product of knowing, ranging from investigation to acquaintance to higher spiritual knowledge.
Arc runs from judicial inquiry and general knowing in classical Greek to a NT-specific sense of higher/esoteric spiritual knowledge; here it names one item in a catalogue of graces to excel in.
This occurrence matches the term's usual NT sense of Christian knowledge/understanding as a virtue to grow in; no divergence.
Occurs here as a noun (dative), one item in a list of nouns naming Christian excellences -- shows the term functions as a named possession/capacity rather than an action.

Semantic range spans judicial inquiry, general knowing, acquaintance with a person, recognition, and higher/esoteric knowledge (a distinctly NT sense) -- here in the sense of Christian understanding as an excellence to grow in.
No disposition/act contrast for this term specifically is shown in this verse; it is listed alongside faith, speech, love, and earnestness as parallel named qualities.
No structural-opposite term (e.g. 'ignorance') appears in this verse's role list.
No person-type term for this characteristic is present in this verse.
No supplication/seeking term for knowledge appears in this verse.
γνῶσις is well attested in classical Greek for knowledge/investigation; the NT develops a specialized sense of higher/spiritual knowledge (Ephesians, 1 Corinthians) building on the classical base.
Not a NT coinage as a term, though its 'higher/esoteric knowledge' nuance is a NT-period semantic development (LSJ notes this NT-specific sub-sense).

Here σπουδή carries its standard sense of earnestness/zeal in a virtue-list, matching its usual NT usage (e.g. Rom.12.8,11; 2Cor.7.11-12); no divergence from the term's ordinary sense.

As a genitive singular noun ('your love'), G0026 here names the Corinthians' own love as the very thing under scrutiny -- an attributed quality being tested for genuineness.
In this verse G0026 means active, self-giving love -- specifically the Corinthians' love expressed through generosity -- whose genuineness Paul is testing.
The term's implication here is constitutional: love is treated as an inner reality that must manifest outwardly (in giving) to be verified as genuine, not merely professed.
The root sense of active, devoted love operates here as the quality Paul wants demonstrated concretely, not merely claimed, by the Corinthians.
This occurrence uses the standard NT sense of active love with no divergence from its usual usage elsewhere in Paul.
G0026 appears here as a noun ('love'), the quality under test, rather than as a verb of loving.
As a genitive noun (N-GSF, 'your love'), G0026 functions here as the possessed quality being examined, grammatically the object of the proving rather than an action.

Here G0026 carries its active, relational sense of self-giving concern (LSJ: love of God for man/man for God, brotherly love), applied to the Corinthians' practical care expressed through the collection.

Within its range from God's love for humanity to interpersonal charity to brotherly love-feasts, this occurrence sits at the interpersonal-charitable sense, love expressed through material generosity toward fellow believers.
This occurrence expresses a quality/disposition (the Corinthians' love as a possessed trait) whose genuineness is being tested, rather than a specific act.
No structural opposite term is invoked in this verse; love here is being tested for genuineness rather than contrasted with an opposing term.
No person-type term (one who habitually loves) is relevant here; the verse addresses the Corinthians' love as a collective quality, not a named class of persons.
No supplication/seeking-term applies here; the verse is about testing existing love, not petitioning for it.

As NT Greek, G0026 here carries the distinctively Christian sense of active, self-giving love (agape) that Paul expects to be verified through concrete generosity, going beyond the term's rarer classical usage.
The specific sense of self-giving, active love as used here is a NT-period semantic development, rare and marginal in pre-NT Greek before becoming central Christian vocabulary in this verse's usage.
γνήσιος names what is 'genuine/legitimate,' rooted in γένος (race/birth) -- signaling authenticity by proper origin, applied here metaphorically to love's sincerity.

As a neuter accusative adjective ('genuine'), G1103 here modifies the noun 'love' abstractly (agreeing with an implied neuter reference), naming the quality of being authentic/legitimate as tested by comparison.
Greek γνήσιος at the definitional level denotes lawfully-born/legitimate, extended to 'genuine, true, unfeigned' of qualities like love or virtue.
In this verse G1103 means true and sincere, as opposed to merely professed -- the standard against which the Corinthians' love is being measured.
The name carries a constitutional implication: authenticity verified by origin/birthright, transferred to mean an inner quality that is not counterfeit.

The term's implication here is constitutional: it asks whether love's inner reality (its essential legitimacy) matches its outward claim, verified through the test of comparison with others' earnestness.
γνήσιος from γένος; root meaning 'belonging to the race/lawfully begotten,' extended figuratively to 'genuine, sincere.'

Rooted in the sense of legitimate birth/lineage extended to authenticity generally, G1103 here operates as the criterion of sincerity that Paul's proving-test seeks to establish for the Corinthians' love.
Arc runs from literal legitimate birth/lawful kinship through legal/social legitimacy (citizens, wives) to figurative 'genuine, true, unfeigned' applied to virtues, writings, and here to love.
This occurrence matches the term's established NT figurative sense ('genuine/sincere' quality); no divergence.
This occurrence uses G1103 in its standard extended sense of 'genuine/sincere' (as elsewhere in the NT of faith or persons), with no divergence here.
Occurs as an adjective here (neuter accusative), modifying 'your love' -- showing the term functions to qualify the authenticity of a named quality rather than stand alone.
G1103 appears here as an adjective ('genuine'), qualifying love as authentic rather than naming an action or process itself.
As an adjective (A-ASN) predicated of 'love,' G1103 functions here to qualify the quality/authenticity of the love in question, not to name an action or disposition in its own right.
Semantic range spans legitimate birth/lawful kinship, true/lawful wives or citizens, unfeigned virtues, and genuine writings/objects -- here applied to love's sincerity, tested by earnestness.
Here G1103 carries its legitimate/authentic sense (LSJ: born-in-wedlock -> real, unfeigned), applied metaphorically to love as sincere rather than merely professed or performed.
Within its range from 'lawfully born' to 'true/sincere' generally, this occurrence sits at the extended moral-sincerity sense, describing love as authentic rather than merely claimed.
γνήσιος functions here as a qualifier of ἀγάπη (love), distinguishing genuine/quality love from its counterfeit rather than naming a disposition of its own.
This occurrence expresses a quality (genuineness as an attribute of love) rather than an act, disposition-in-process, or received condition.
No structural-opposite term (e.g. 'counterfeit/false') is present in this verse's role list.

G1103's structural opposite (implied by the test itself) is feigned or merely professed love; the verse's whole logic depends on the genuine/counterfeit contrast even though the negative term is not lexically present.

No person-type term (one who habitually possesses genuineness) is relevant here; the word qualifies an abstract quality (love), not a class of persons.

γνήσιος is classical Greek (Homer onward) for legitimate birth, continued in NT with the extended sense 'genuine/sincere.'

As NT Greek, this occurrence extends the term's classical sense (legitimate birth, true lineage) metaphorically to moral/spiritual authenticity, fitting Paul's use of it to describe sincere love verified by test.
Not a NT coinage; attested from Homer and classical prose/poetry.

G1103 is attested from at least the 8th century BC (Homer) for 'lawfully born, genuine,' so this occurrence continues an established classical sense extended metaphorically rather than being a NT coinage.
δοκιμάζω names the act of 'testing/proving,' rooted in δόκιμος (approved) -- signaling verification through trial, here applied to testing the genuineness of love.
As a present active participle ('proving/testing'), G1381 here names Paul's act of using others' zeal as a testing-standard, not a completed verdict but an ongoing act of assay.
Greek δοκιμάζω at the definitional level denotes assaying/testing (metals, persons) and by extension approving after scrutiny.
In this verse G1381 means to test or assay by comparison, as Paul appeals to the earnestness of others as a proving-standard against which the Corinthians' love can be measured.
The name carries a relational implication: an evaluative act performed by one party assessing another's quality by an external standard (here, the earnestness of others).

Here the testing is directional: it moves from the example of others' earnestness toward a verdict on the genuineness of the Corinthians' own love, functioning as an external benchmark rather than a command.
δοκιμάζω, from δόκιμος, root meaning 'assay, test, put to proof' -- of metals, persons, or claims.
The root sense of assaying/testing operates here as Paul tests the reality of the Corinthians' love by holding it against the earnestness already shown by others.
Arc runs from literal assaying of metals/coins through testing of persons and political scrutiny for office to NT moral-testing of professed virtues, as here with love's genuineness.
This occurrence matches the term's usual sense of testing/proving a claimed quality; no divergence.
This occurrence uses the standard testing/proving sense of G1381 with no divergence from its usual usage elsewhere.
Occurs here as a present participle ('to prove'), showing the term functions verbally as an ongoing act of testing performed by Paul via the letter.
G1381 occurs here as a present active participle ('proving'), showing the characteristic operating as an ongoing evaluative act performed by the speaker rather than as a static noun-quality.

As a present active participle (V-PAP-NSM), G1381 modifies Paul's speech-act ('I say this... to prove'), showing the testing as an ongoing purpose behind his statement rather than a discrete finished act.

Semantic range spans assaying metals/coins, testing persons, political scrutiny for office, and approval after examination -- here in the sense of testing/proving the genuineness of a moral quality (love) via comparison.

In this verse G1381 carries its testing/examining sense (LSJ: assay, put to the test), used here specifically to verify the sincerity of a professed virtue (love) by comparison with a benchmark (others' earnestness).

Within its semantic range from assaying metals to scrutinizing persons for fitness, this occurrence sits at the interpersonal-comparative end: testing the genuineness of one group's love via another's example.
The term names an act (testing) distinct from the disposition being tested (love's genuineness), showing act-versus-quality distinction functionally in this verse.
This occurrence expresses an act (the testing performed by Paul) rather than a disposition or received condition.

The characteristic named from ὀκνηρός ('slothful, hesitant, timid') is the disposition-pole of the M67 cluster, signaling a shrinking-back or reluctance rooted in timidity/fear rather than mere inactivity.

ὀκνηρός derives from ὄκνος ('hesitation, shrinking, fear'). LSJ's core sense is 'shrinking, timid', especially from fear, opposed to τολμηρός ('bold'); secondarily 'idle, sluggish'. Mounce/tree give 'lazy, idle, not active; troublesome'.

The word carries a relational/directional implication toward action or engagement that is being avoided or shrunk from -- LSJ's 'causing fear, vexatious, troublesome' sense (of things) shows the term can describe not only the timid person but the burdensome task from which one shrinks.
Primary Greek term ὀκνηρός, from ὄκνος ('hesitation/timidity/fear'). Root meaning: shrinking back from fear, hence reluctant, sluggish, slothful. No Hebrew equivalent supplied for this NT-only term.

The full arc runs from military/psychological timidity (shrinking from danger, opposed to boldness) through general idleness/sluggishness to, in its single NT occurrence, a moral exhortation against spiritual/relational sloth as the opposite pole to the zeal (ζῆλος) commanded in the same verse.

In Rom.12.11 ὀκνηρός sits within its base gloss ('slothful, indolent') with no notable surface divergence -- the exhortation 'do not be slothful in zeal' uses the term in its standard moral-ethical sense as attested elsewhere (e.g. Matt 25:26), so no shift is recorded.
This occurrence matches ὀκνηρός's usual 'lazy/idle' sense as in Mt.25.26, with no divergence in nuance here.

ὀκνηρός is an adjective (A-NPM in this occurrence), modifying persons directly ('be not slothful [ones]'), showing the characteristic operates as a state/disposition ascribed to a person rather than an isolated act.

Semantic range spans fear-rooted timidity/hesitation before action (LSJ's primary sense, opposed to τολμηρός 'bold'), general idleness/sluggishness, and (of things) 'vexatious, troublesome' -- describing what causes reluctance as well as the reluctant disposition itself.

None distinct within this occurrence; ὀκνηρός itself functions substantivally when applied directly to persons, but no separate agent-noun form is attested here.
None. No supplication/seeking term for overcoming sloth is present among these occurrences; the exhortation is a direct imperative ('do not be...') rather than a petition.

No Hebrew counterpart supplied; the term's development is intra-Greek, moving from a fear-rooted psychological/military sense in classical usage (soldiers 'more timid' in battle, LSJ) to a general moral exhortation against sluggishness in the Christian life in its sole NT occurrence.
None. ὀκνηρός is attested from classical sources (Pindar, Xenophon, Demosthenes per LSJ), not coined in the NT period.

σπουδή derives from σπεύδω ('to hasten'). LSJ shows the primary sense as physical 'haste, speed', extending to 'zeal, pains, trouble, effort' and 'earnestness' as a serious, engaged disposition contrasted with playfulness (παιδιά). Mounce/tree agree: haste, diligence, enthusiasm, zeal.

The full arc moves from concrete physical haste/speed, through general zealous exertion and attentiveness (including political/partisan zeal in classical usage), to an ethical-relational sense in the NT epistles where earnestness becomes visible proof of sincere character (repentance, love, generosity) offered for others to observe and judge.

In Mark.6.25 σπουδή retains its base literal sense of physical haste ('with haste' to the king) with no metaphorical shift. In 2Cor.7.11, 7.12, 8.7, 8.8 and Rom.12.11 the term shifts from physical speed to an ethical-relational nuance of demonstrable zeal/earnestness functioning as evidence of sincerity -- a marked shift from the base 'haste' gloss toward a virtue-term describing wholehearted moral engagement, distinctive to the Pauline corpus's use compared to the narrative/literal use in Mark.

This occurrence matches σπουδή's established religious-zeal sense (cf. Rom.12.8, Heb.6.11) rather than its more common secular 'haste' sense; no additional divergence beyond that already-attested religious usage.

σπουδή occurs here only as a noun (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-ASF, N-DSF across occurrences), naming a quality or state rather than the act itself; the related adverb σπουδαίως (G4709) supplies the manner-of-action form, showing the characteristic operates both as a describable quality possessed and as a manner in which action is carried out.

Semantic range spans literal physical haste/speed (Mark 6:25, 'with haste' to the king), zeal as attentive/earnest effort in relationships and undertakings (Rom 12:11, 'not lagging in zeal'), and a demonstrable, quasi-evidentiary sense -- earnestness that others can observe and that functions as proof of genuine character (2 Cor 7:11-12, 8:7-8, where σπουδή is offered as evidence of repentance and love alongside other virtues).

The structural opposites within this cluster's own vocabulary are ἀργός (G0692, idle/ineffective) and ὀκνηρός (G3636, slothful/reluctant) -- both name the deficiency or absence that σπουδή positively fills.
Called 'mercy/show mercy' (eleeō) in the programme; the name signals an active response of compassion enacted toward one in need, not merely felt pity.

Primary term eleeō, rooted in eleos ('pity'); root meaning shows compassion directed toward another's suffering translated into an act of mercy.
Full arc runs from felt pity to active mercy-showing to (absolute use) simply 'feeling pity'; in this verse it sits at the active, habitual-practice end as one of several enumerated spiritual gifts.
This occurrence matches the term's usual sense (active mercy-showing) as elsewhere in the NT (e.g. Jude 22-23); no divergent nuance beyond the standard sense.

The verse itself supplies the disposition/manner distinction: the verb names the act (doing mercy) while the accompanying dative 'with cheerfulness' distinguishes the manner/disposition in which the act should be carried out.
No structural-opposite term for mercy is present in this verse's vocabulary.

Primary term metadidōmi, root meta- ('with/share') + didōmi ('give'); root meaning shows sharing a part of what one possesses with another.
Full arc runs from sharing material goods/offices/rights to communicating information; in this verse it sits at the material-sharing end, one of the enumerated spiritual gifts.
This occurrence matches the term's usual sense elsewhere in the NT (e.g. Luke 3:11, Eph 4:28) of sharing material resources; no divergence.
Grammatical range is verbal; here a present participle ('the one who contributes'), naming a habitual gift-function/person-type rather than a single act.
Semantic range covers sharing possessions, distributing goods, and communicating/imparting information; here it names the material-sharing sense within the list of spiritual gifts.

Greek paraklesis at the definitional level shows a call-to-one's-aid/summons root, ranging through exhortation, entreaty, and consolation -- the same term covers urging to action and comforting in distress.

This occurrence uses paraklesis in its standard hortatory-instruction sense (paired with 'the one who exhorts'), matching the term's usual Rom 12 sense rather than diverging toward the consolation nuance found elsewhere (e.g. 2Cor 1, Luke 2:25).

Here G3874 is a feminine noun (N-DSF, dative of manner/sphere) -- this occurrence shows the term operating as the named quality/mode attached to the participial gift-function 'the one who exhorts', i.e. abstract noun paired with a verbal role.

Semantic range spans hortatory instruction/incitement, earnest supplication/appeal, and consolation/comfort/solace -- in combination with 'the one who exhorts' here it sits at the hortatory-instruction end of that range, not the consolation end.

Paraklesis is attested pre-NT (classical Greek summons/appeal/exhortation sense, Demosthenes, Thucydides) with the consolation sense appearing in LXX (Isa 30:7, Nah 3:7) and carried into NT -- shows continuity of the term with development of its consolation nuance strengthened in NT/LXX usage.

The characteristic is named spoudē, 'zeal/earnestness/diligence' (also 'haste'). The name signals intense, energetic devotion applied toward a task or relationship, the noun form of the same root as G4709.

Greek spoudē at the definitional level denotes 'haste, speed,' extending to 'zeal, pains, effort, earnestness' and even 'esteem, regard' for a person — showing the term bridges swift physical motion and sustained moral/relational diligence.

The name carries a relational implication: spoudē is regularly directed toward a person, cause, or goal (zeal 'in leading,' eagerness 'to write,' earnestness 'to have full assurance') — it is constitutionally other-directed or goal-directed rather than self-contained.

Primary Greek term spoudē (from speudō, 'to hasten') shows a root meaning of urgent forward motion that develops into sustained zealous effort and even esteem/regard for persons. No Hebrew term is supplied in these sources.

The vocabulary arc for spoudē runs from physical haste/speed, through effortful diligence and zealous exertion in tasks, to personal esteem/regard, religious zeal, and full assurance of hope — showing the term's capacity to describe both the manner of action and the intensity of relational/spiritual commitment across these three occurrences (leadership, writing urgency, and hope-related diligence).
This occurrence sits within the base gloss 'zeal/diligence' as the manner accompanying leadership - no notable divergence from the general stepGloss.

Grammatical range is nominal (N-DSF/N-ASF), functioning as the object of prepositions ('with zeal', 'with haste') or as direct object of verbs ('show earnestness'), showing the characteristic operates as a quality or manner brought to bear on an action rather than an action itself.

The vocabulary arc runs from concrete economic idleness (unemployed persons, fallow fields, unworked money) through social censure (busybody idlers going house to house, 1Tim 5:13; lazy gluttons, Titus 1:12) to abstract theological application (useless/ineffective faith without works, Jas 2:20) — showing a single root sense of 'non-functioning' extended across physical, social, and spiritual domains.

Grammatical range is adjectival (A-NPF etc.), used substantivally ('idlers') or predicatively ('is no trouble', 'is useless'). This shows the characteristic operates as a descriptor of persons, things, or states rather than as a verbal action in its own right.

This term names 'earnest promptness' (spoudaiōs) in the M67 programme -- the adverb signals urgent, energetic care applied to practical assistance of others, here Paul's instruction concerning Zenas and Apollos.
